source.title: Model Stitching: Looking For Functional Similarity Between Representations
source.authors: Adriano Hernandez; Rumen Dangovski; Peter Y. Lu; Marin Soljačić

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendix, is present. The result tables are flattened in the supplied text, making some groupings of their numerical entries unclear.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether learned stitches make representations functionally interchangeable, a conceptual test of V4. It also reports conditions under which stitching accuracy may not reliably indicate representational similarity.
record.gate_note: The paper trains stitches between CIFAR-10 ResNets and reports their downstream accuracy as a similarity measure, plus representational MSE sanity tests. Background discussion and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. Stitched-accuracy grids are mostly shown in figures; the text describes their qualitative pattern but gives no exact stitched-accuracy values.
record.test_reason: The study stitches every ordered pair of 16 CIFAR-10 ResNet architectures, plus ResNet18 and ResNet34, and uses stitched accuracy as a similarity measure. This bears on V4, whether representations can be swapped through a learned stitch. It also bears on V6: stitching rates distant layers as highly similar, while representation-matching (MSE-trained) stitches give a different picture. The authors argue that naive stitching may not measure similarity.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find high stitch accuracy whenever the receiver layer is proportionally earlier than the sender layer, even for distant layers, and the pattern extends to ResNet18/34. They hypothesize that stitches 'hack' the receiver rather than match its expected representation, so naive stitching may not measure similarity accurately. Their MSE sanity tests cannot confirm this hypothesis. They still regard functional stitching as better than geometric or statistical measures.
record.recipe_differences: Uses model stitching and downstream task accuracy as in prior stitching work, extending comparisons to different ResNet architectures and layer shapes. The study trains stitches for four epochs and uses CIFAR-10 Small ResNets; it also includes random-network controls and MSE sanity tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Stitching accuracy depends on the relative sender and receiver layer positions and direction; the reported high-similarity region is a proportional lower-left triangle. The text also notes directional differences associated with upsampling and downsampling.
record.problems: The main similarity results are presented as accuracy grids rather than numerical tables, and exact stitched accuracies are not stated in the text. The models share CIFAR-10 training data and task, so the study cannot distinguish explanations based on shared data or objectives. The authors say the MSE sanity tests are inconclusive about the hacking hypothesis; the flattened tables also make detailed numeric assignments unclear.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result bearing on the claim was intentionally left out. The numerical MSE tables are summarized in aggregate because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve all cell groupings.

untested.parts: Linear maps, relative representations, unpaired mapping, and other architectures or modalities. Only convolutional stitches between CIFAR-10 ResNets are tested.
No comparison of CKA or other standard metrics, no neighbour settings, and no out-of-distribution inputs.
No test of alignment against model scale.
No feature- or subspace-level analysis across seeds.
No analysis of shared data or objectives as the cause of alignment.

missing.what: Similarity-trained (MSE) stitches give low task accuracy, versus about 90% for vanilla stitches in the triangle, even when trained 30 epochs against 4. This contrast underpins the V4 limit and the V6 view that a representation-matching map measures something different from stitch accuracy.
missing.locator: Appendix, Numerical Sanity Testing; Figure 5 caption

missing.what: Diagonal (corresponding-layer) stitching gives the same high accuracy as Bansal et al. This is the clean V4 condition and is not separated from the distant-layer triangle in r1.

record.verdict_notes: No V6 verdict is given. The study's own evidence for metric dependence is only suggestive: high stitch accuracy between distant layers, which the authors find implausible, alongside MSE tests they call inconclusive. Under these rules that is not a clear limits_scope or challenges, and supports would overstate it. r2, r5 and r6 are relinked to V6 for reference, and the Figure 5 contrast is listed under missing. All models share CIFAR-10 and the classification task. The main results appear only in figures, with qualitative text descriptions. This is a short workshop-style preprint, and the stitched-accuracy values come from a figure caption.

versions.untested_parts: No test of alignment rising with model size and capability across independently trained models.
No vision-language or paired image-caption comparison.
The study varies architecture, but does not report independently trained seeds of the same architecture learning shared features or subspaces.
Tests learned stitching between ResNet representations; does not test linear maps, stitching across other architectures or modalities, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are identified.
Tests stitching accuracy across layer pairings and reports MSE sanity checks, but does not compare a range of similarity metrics, neighbour settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
All trained models use CIFAR-10 and the paper does not separate the effects of shared data or objectives from other explanations for alignment.

rows.operation_detail: Train stitches between every ordered pair of Small ResNets and measure stitched-network downstream accuracy.

conditions.value: sender layer i and receiver layer j, where j is proportionally before i in the receiver network (Jj ≤ Ii)

rows.measure: stitched-network CIFAR-10 accuracy, used as similarity
rows.baseline: Original trained networks each have accuracy above 90%.
rows.value: High stitching accuracy; exact values not stated. The text describes high similarity for each sender layer to receiver layers proportionally before it.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result stated for trained Small ResNets; the individual layer-pair values are plotted, not tabulated.
rows.check: A value is available. The Figure 5 caption says vanilla stitches reach 'very high similarity near 90%' in the lower-left triangle, against original accuracy above 90%. Subjects are different architectures that differ only by initialization. The triangle covers distant, non-corresponding layers, so for V4 the observed state mixes the expected corresponding-layer interchange with the result the authors call perplexing.

source_check.correct: V4: observed. This result alone cannot determine V6 because it does not compare similarity measures or input distributions. Figure 5 additionally describes vanilla stitching accuracy near 90%; individual layer-pair accuracies are not stated numerically.
source_check.problem: The observed state fits V4, but the row alone does not establish the metric or data dependence asserted by V6.

rows.operation_detail: Compare mean-squared errors (MSE) for expected representations and representations produced by vanilla or similarity-trained stitches.

conditions.value: EV: expected versus vanilla-stitch output; ES: expected versus similarity-trained-stitch output; SV: similarity-trained versus vanilla-stitch output

rows.baseline: Similarity-trained stitch is trained to minimize ES MSE; the text treats this as a reference for low MSE.
rows.value: Table 1 reports minimum, mean, maximum, and standard deviation for EV, ES, and SV. The text says the predicted ordering is typically present, but not sufficiently large or common to conclude that vanilla stitches are likely hacking the receiver.
rows.uncertainty: Minimum, mean, maximum, and standard deviation are reported; exact cell assignments cannot be reliably recovered from the flattened table.
rows.note: The table contains multiple blocks of numbers whose groupings are unclear in the supplied flattened layout. The row records the authors' explicit summary rather than assigning ambiguous individual values.
rows.check: These are MSE sanity checks comparing vanilla stitches with similarity-trained stitches. The ordering the authors predicted typically holds but is not large, so the results are inconclusive about the hacking hypothesis. They bear on whether stitch accuracy reflects representational match (V6), not on V4 interchangeability itself.
